results.explanationEn: The text says that four months earlier he considered the policy natural, but he has changed so much that he is now ashamed of it. It then says the days passing over his head brought broader, more mature views and faith in the fleet, so the answer is A. B misreads the phrase as storms. C's orders and D's aging and illness have no support in the text.

The aunt knew the dish was too salty but said nothing, either at the table or in the car. On the salt flat she shows Shirin the soil preserved moist beneath the salt crust, says "salt covers, and it keeps," and carefully wraps a piece to take home. Putting these together, the salt crust symbolizes the aunt's choice to cover the mistake while keeping it as a lesson, so the answer is D. A does not match the aunt's actual reaction, and B and C connect to the salt only on the surface.

The clause explains that the early painting remained beneath the new layer of paint and was revealed by infrared imaging, so the original was hidden but preserved intact, not destroyed. Therefore "conceal" is closest to hide, meaning to cover or keep out of sight. Destroy contradicts the fact that the original was still found. Revise would mean the original was altered, which differs from a situation where it was fully painted over. Duplicate means something entirely different.

Earlier, Layla shows the habit of filling Tamar's jar before her own every day, even during the week she could not teach because of a cough. After the blank, even the day after her son's ship returns, she fills the jar at the same hour on the rooftop, which shows it was not a pretext for watching the sea. The choice that satisfies both constraints is a steady devotion, so the answer is D. A borrows the text's theme word "pretext" and does not fit the sentence's reversal. B is too weak and conflicts with a daily habit. C fits only the earlier scene of watching the harbor.

This study is an observational study of which route commuters chose for themselves, and the commuters were not randomly assigned to routes with or without bus lanes. So the difference in commute time between the two groups (28.4 minutes vs. 35.7 minutes) might be an effect of the bus lanes, but it might also be due to other confounding variables, such as people who prefer shorter routes having chosen roads with bus lanes in the first place. Therefore a causal relationship cannot be asserted, and the answer is D. A is wrong because the fact that the sample sizes differ does not by itself invalidate the comparison (a simple comparison of averages is still possible). B is untrue because the data are already given consistently in minutes. C is unrelated to the core problem of an observational study, the absence of random assignment.

Early in the text, the narrator makes excited jokes about the basketball hoop being the most loyal audience and hands over a gift. But when Samira returns the gift without opening it and says she will not need it in Milan, the narrator looks at the worn floor where people paused and then turned away. So the tone moves from bright optimism to a quiet sense of loss, and the answer is A. In C, there is no scene of the narrator resenting or forgiving anyone. In D, Milan is mentioned, but the excited plans are Samira's and are the opposite of the narrator's feelings.
Subtracting 150 from both sides gives $-12y = 6 - 150 = -144$. Dividing both sides by $-12$ gives $y = \frac{-144}{-12} = 12$. So 12 bottles were filled.

The first part sets a comfortable mood with a pleasant daily conversation about the wind, the herons, and the glittering salt piles. When the boy asks why Bruno does not wear a ring, the bus falls silent, and Isadora feels ashamed that she knew Bruno's rehearsed answer and was grateful for it. So C, which moves from easy, comfortable routine to an uneasy sense of evasion exposed, is the answer. D reverses the order of sorrow and amusement in the text, and A is wrong because there is no scene in which Bruno becomes honest.

The point where the arch's height is 0 is an x-intercept. Since $f(x) = -x^2+8x-7 = -(x^2-8x+7) = -(x-1)(x-7)$, the values where $f(x)=0$ are $x=1$ and $x=7$. In the graph, you can see that the parabola opens downward (concave down, with a maximum point) and crosses the x-axis twice, near 1 and 7. So the answer is D.

The writer imagines a person who does not know the language and considers in turn that speech and dictionaries are of no use. Then he declares, "Clearly there is but one possible way," and presents a method that uses the senses. So the answer is D, confident and logical. A is wrong because he finds a method of communication, and B and C are wrong because there is no language dismissing the stranger or finding him amusing.

Just before the underlined sentence, Jakub says he wrote the song. The underlined sentence shows that Eitan wrote the bridge on the back of a parking ticket and still carries that paper in his pocket. Combined with the later scene in which Jakub splits the coins evenly and treats fairness as arithmetic, this sharpens the unfairness of the credit. So the answer is A. The lost money in B, the solo authorship in C, and the weather description in D have no support in the text.

The text explains that the scraper was left to Eulalio, who once insulted the master's bread, and not to Meera, his student of twenty years. Scenes follow in which customers whisper, Eulalio avoids eye contact, and he finally leaves it at Meera's door, so a medal pinned on the wrong chest means an honor that belonged to someone else. So the answer is A. B reads the medal literally as a prize, C has no support, and D does not match Eulalio's shrinking behavior.

The first part shows the proud success of two children bringing the orchard back to life together, and the latter part contrasts this with the landlord father and the tenant mother starting to argue over profits and debts, so that the children, too, begin counting fruit before telling stories. So B, which says a shared success drew a friendship into two families' tensions, is the answer. A only summarizes the episode, and C uses the subject matter but makes a claim the text does not contain as its purpose. D is an overly general lesson.

The question asks for the new finding that most directly supports the claim that electric trolleys, not income growth, drove outlying residential development. The text mentions that income growth could also be an alternative explanation, so evidence that rules out this alternative is needed. Correct choice B shows that construction surged right after trolley lines opened even in areas where household income had not yet risen, which directly shows that trolley access, not income, was the cause. A merely repeats a fact already in the text (the increase in construction in Cleveland) and does not rule out the income variable. C shows only that trolley speeds increased and does not show that this was a cause taking precedence over income growth. D is only background that outlying areas were once considered unsuitable for development and does not answer whether income or trolleys was the cause. So the answer is B.

The letters were all written to Noor but never mailed, and they confess that the grandfather took her poem as his own. Also, Faris has twice heard Noor say with a laugh that his grandfather never apologized. Connecting these clues, he meant to deliver the apology she never received, so the answer is C. A draws a different feeling from the confession, and D mistakes Noor's reading and stopping her knitting for his motive. B borrows only the snowstorm detail as an outside reason.

Correct choice C: it states the directly counted "38 percent decrease" definitively, while presenting the explanation that noise interferes with the vibrations tentatively, as a proposal she did not test directly, so it accurately distinguishes the certainty of the two points.
A (overstatement): it writes the untested noise hypothesis with "because," as if Lindqvist had proved the causal link.
B (understatement): it needlessly weakens the directly confirmed decrease in visits with "may have," and it also drops the 38 percent figure.
D (confusion): it handles the levels of certainty correctly, but the explanation it gives, road dust and scent detection, wrongly moves a separate study by Ortiz (which was also on honeybees) into Lindqvist's study.

Before the underlined sentence, Marcus shrugs at the news of the museum selection and says several times that the quilt is just scraps. But in the underlined sentence, he folds the quilt so that the tag embroidered with his name is the first thing seen by whoever opens the box, so the answer is C: a detail that quietly undercuts his claim of indifference. The final scene, in which the narrator notices this and pretends not to, also supports this reading. D focuses on the relationship between the brothers, but the narrator shows generosity, not resentment, and A and B do not match the text.

Connecting the sentence saying Noor finished in four minutes a repair that used to take a long time with the underlined sentence, in which Layla awkwardly keeps wiping the same corner of the lens for a long time, we can tell she is hiding her feelings. The later scene in which she says to herself, almost as an aside, that the timing was "fine" also supports an unspoken compliment. So the answer is D. A contradicts the fact that the repair was fast, B reads the lens wiping only literally, and C is wrong because the text has no development in which a conflict is resolved.

Correct choice B presents together that the underdrawings were apprentice-style yet the final brushwork did not match the master's technique, and that the compositions and colors still followed the master's typical style. This precisely supports the execution-based view that stylistic consistency (composition and color) alone cannot show whether the master actually painted a work and that separate evidence of execution, namely brushwork, is needed. A is a trap: it pairs apprentice underdrawings with brushwork that matches the master, a combination in the opposite direction not in the text, and it can seem to support the stylistic view (matching composition and color is enough). C pairs master-style underdrawings with mismatched brushwork, a combination not in the text, and it undermines the reliability of the execution-based standard by shaking the correlation between underdrawing and brushwork, so it does not support that view. D presents only that composition and color match and does not mention brushwork (evidence of execution), so it actually supports the opposing view that stylistic consistency is enough.

The text explains that the contrast of light and dark is not mere decoration but focuses the viewer's gaze on a particular figure's emotional expression, creating dramatic urgency. This means it "raises" the emotional intensity, that is, strengthens it, so intensify is the answer. Elevate physically is the literal meaning of heighten, but it does not fit here because the subject is emotion. Lengthen concerns time or length and is unrelated to the context, and publicize means something entirely different.

Early on, the siblings are exuberant: they have sold all the kites, Yuxuan gives the pawnbroker an exaggerated greeting, and Shanice laughs so hard she drops the bundle. After reading the letters, the mood turns heavy and unsettled: Yuxuan goes to bed without brushing his teeth, and Shanice forgets the kettle twice. So the answer is B. A and C reverse the direction of the change or assume the letters gave answers, and D invents conflict between the siblings.

The text explicitly contrasts the city's decline as "not a sudden shock but a gradual erosion." The following sentences also explain that orders "slowly dwindled year after year" and that workers left in "a steady trickle rather than a mass exodus," emphasizing that the change proceeded as if being worn away bit by bit. So erosion is best matched by "Gradual wearing away," meaning slowly worn down and lost. "Sudden interruption" carries the sense of suddenness that the text denies, so it is the opposite (OPPOSITE_CONNOTATION). "Overall decline" is right about the result of decline but misses the key nuance of gradualness that this word emphasizes (RELATED_BUT_WRONG_FIT). "Widespread depletion" means the exhaustion of resources, a different meaning that does not fit the context of the text (WRONG_SENSE).

Step 1: Substituting $x=1$ gives $p+q=10$.
Step 2: Substituting $x=2$ gives $8p+4q=56$, and dividing both sides by 4 gives $2p+q=14$.
Step 3: Subtracting the two equations gives $p=4$, so $q=6$.
Step 4: The expression is $4x^3+6x^2$, and factoring out the common factor $2x^2$ gives $2x^2(2x+3)$. The answer is A.
Wrong choice B: it swaps $p$ and $q$. Expanding it gives $6x^3+4x^2$.
Wrong choice C: it wrongly factors out $2x^3$. Expanding it gives $4x^4+6x^3$, whose exponents do not match the original expression.
Wrong choice D: it finds only $p=4$ and uses the sum $p+q=10$ in place of $q$. Expanding it gives $4x^3+10x^2$.

The writer says the professional criminal is not noticeable in a mixed crowd except to those who know him, and then contrasts this with the tramp. So saying the tramp can be picked out in a crowd means he is easily recognized by almost anyone, and the answer is A. B misreads "pick" as selection, and C and D take "crowd" literally.

"Each material" is treated as singular, so the pronoun that refers back to it must also be singular, and the verb "contributes" already agrees in the singular form. "It" satisfies this singular agreement. "They" and "them" are plural pronouns and do not agree in number with "each material," and "materials" is not a pronoun but a repetition of the noun, creating unnecessary redundancy and an awkward appositive structure.

A lantern lights the way ahead, while a stone is a burden to carry, so the metaphor means that the truth helps the boy find his way rather than weighing him down. This is supported by the younger brother, who, after hearing the truth, cries and then asks increasingly practical questions, and the next day chooses a path himself and walks ahead. A stays at the comparison of weight and misses the guiding sense of "lantern." B misreads it as the adult carrying the burden in his place, and D has no support in the text, so C is the answer.

While rummaging through a pile of clothes, he happens upon a pickaxe he had kept for a year and forgotten. The pickaxe is the proof he was looking for, so "resurrection" means that forgotten proof has suddenly reappeared. So the answer is A. B does not match the fact that the pickaxe came out of the pile of clothes, and C and D misread the metaphor literally.

The text first describes a small animal giving off a fierce look. Then Bella scolds the animal and strokes it, and instead of attacking, it plays like a kitten. So B, which captures the process from fierce look to being calmed by kindness, is the answer. A is wrong because Bella is not afraid, and C and D differ from the text in order and content.

Reading letters that record tomato prices and neighbors' quarrels instead of the recipe, the narrator cannot stop laughing at the line "stir until it tells you," which appears in an unrelated context. She then thinks her mother left the recipe not on paper but in her children. Connecting the two clues, B, which expresses fond amusement, is the answer. A has no evidence that the mother hid it on purpose, C ignores the emotional response, and the guilt in D is not shown.

Most of the poem is filled with calm, reverent images such as the rules of the hive, slow breathing movements, and a bee walking across a wrist. Grief shows briefly where the husband's name catches in her throat and the yard goes quiet for a moment, but soon the smoke and the sound of bees return. So C, calm reverence touched by a brief note of grief, is the answer. A mentions only the less prominent grief, B reverses the proportions, and D fits the subject of bees but has no clue of playful curiosity.

Moira admits that she still wanted Samira's blessing and follows exactly what she learned from Samira, to state the verdict plainly. At the same time she states her decision clearly, "I am going," so both respect and self-assertion show, and the answer is C. A is wrong because it ignores the teachings, and B is wrong because it misses the seriousness of acknowledging the real cause of the quarrel. D is wrong because she apologizes but keeps her decision to leave.

This sentence has a structure in which two verb phrases, "speeds embryonic development" and "(thereby) shortens the incubation period," are joined by the conjunction "and" inside a single clause whose subject is "warmer water." "Thereby" is an adverb that merely modifies the following verb "shortens" and does not introduce an independent clause, so no comma or semicolon is needed before or after it. B puts an unnecessary comma after "and," setting off "thereby" as if it were a parenthetical. C puts commas on both sides and over-separates it. D uses a semicolon, treating "thereby shortens..." as if it were an independent clause, which violates the clause-boundary rule that a semicolon requires. So A, which connects them smoothly as "and thereby" with no punctuation, is the answer.

The singular noun ledger must be possessive, so an apostrophe is needed (ledger's), and the plural subject entries needs the plural verb were. No unnecessary comma goes between "entries" and "were written in multiple hands."

Early in the poem, the speaker grumbles that the bread is late and the crust is soft, and says Felix wrote the coins Mio stole in the ledger. The correction in the middle, "I do not keep a ledger, exactly," shows that the speaker has not forgotten the incident. But later the speaker leaves the side door open, pours Mio's second cup in advance, and pushes it over without opening the ledger, so C, accepting Mio while keeping the old wrong in mind, is the answer. A and D read only the grumbling tone, and B changes the reason for the kindness to guilt over Felix.

The uncle regarded Nora as a rival, but when a warp thread snaps, she helps him finish the cloth by tying the thread across. The line that neither the still warp nor the crossing weft alone makes a cloth symbolizes opposing sides joining to form one whole. So the answer is A. B, C, and D take the rules in the first line, the debt, and the rivalry from the text, but they do not match the joining that the thread imagery points to.

Line $j$ has a $y$-intercept of $-3$ and a slope of $1$ on the graph, so $y = x - 3$. Line $k$ is $y = -x + 1$. Solving the two equations together gives $x - 3 = -x + 1$, so $2x = 4$, that is, $x = 2$. So the $x$-coordinate of the intersection of the two lines is $2$.

What comes before the blank is a complete independent clause (Some planners proposed elevated tracks), and what comes after is a noun phrase with no verb (a solution that promised...). For this kind of dependent modifying phrase, it is standard to use a participle (offering) joined with a comma, so D is the answer. A uses a relative clause (which offered), but it may look fine because the verb offered follows which; since "a solution" that follows is already a noun phrase, "which offered a solution" creates a double predicate and is awkward. B has no punctuation at all, so the boundary between the independent clause and the participial phrase is unclear. C puts a participial phrase, not an independent clause, after a semicolon, which breaks the rule for using semicolons. So the answer is D.

Early on, she recalls the forest where she first met Harcourt and feels "wistfulness and regret." But after "But more bewildering than all," she realizes she has been portrayed through her lover's eyes and feels sweet flattery and a pleased thrill. So the answer is A. The anger in B, the suspicion in C, and the boredom in D do not appear in the text.

The speaker compares every bowl leaning toward the window to seedlings seeking light and views with affection a feature the family does not notice. The speaker then does not say so, taking the careful stance of a guest, saying some knowing belongs to the hands that made it. So the answer is C. A is wrong because there is no language criticizing the family's arguing, and B is wrong because envy is not shown. D is wrong because the speaker already understands the meaning of the tilt.

The text explains that a conservator found the same unfinished pattern in several preliminary sketches and concluded that it was a deliberate choice, not an accident. So "calculated" is used to mean intentional or planned, and "deliberate" is the closest. "Numerical" relates to numbers and is irrelevant to the context, "cautious" means careful and does not fit the context of artistic intent, and "unexpected" means not anticipated, the opposite of the intentionality the text emphasizes.
